@graph.headline: C-DAC’s 10,000-unit AI compute tender is a first stage, not a deployment count
@graph.description: C-DAC seeks AI compute providers in two stages. The 10,000-unit figure is a tender requirement, not deployed capacity or a completed purchase.

acceptedAnswer.text: The RFE seeks services using up to 10,000 AI compute units, and defines a unit as a hardware device that can include GPUs, accelerators, TPUs and similar equipment. It is an empanelment followed by Stage-2 procurement, not proof that 10,000 GPUs have been purchased or deployed. C-DAC may also scale capacity above 10,000 based on demand.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Stage 1 and Stage 2?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stage 1 is technical qualification and empanelment. The RFE says it does not seek service-level requirements or financial bids at that stage. Stage 2 is procurement of AI compute services through GeM from empanelled providers, when C-DAC will determine the engagement model, quantities and award strategy. Passing Stage 1 does not guarantee work.

mainEntity.name: When are bids due and when will they open?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 27 October 2026 C-DAC corrigendum changes the dates in the original RFE. Bid submission now ends on 13 November 2026 at 3:30 p.m. IST, and bid opening is scheduled for 14 November at 4 p.m. IST. This report uses the amended dates and does not repeat the superseded 29–30 October timetable.

mainEntity.name: Does the tender promise five years of service for 10,000 units?

acceptedAnswer.text: The RFE describes AI compute services for five years and an initial requirement of up to 10,000 AI compute units, with potential demand-based expansion. Those terms do not amount to a confirmed five-year award for every unit. Provider selection, quantities, start dates and final service terms depend on Stage-2 procurement and later agreements.

No. The RFE describes an initial requirement of up to 10,000 units but also says C-DAC may scale total capacity beyond 10,000 during the empanelment validity according to demand. That is permission to expand, not a forecast or guarantee that the final capacity will exceed the initial request.
